They have five hydroxy groups and one aldehyde group with six carbon atoms all together. It is a white, crystalline, sweet-tasting substance that is highly soluble in water.
2. Oligosaccharides
Oligosaccharides (G. oligo = a few) are the chains of 2 to 10 monosaccharides linked by
glycosidic bonds. They generally taste sweet and are water soluble. Some important
oligosaccharides are:

The most abundant oligosaccharides in the animal and plant cells are the disaccharides such as sucrose, maltose and lactose. Raffinose (C18H32O16) is made of three sugar molecules: galactose, glucose, and fructose. Stachyose (C24H42O21) is made of four sugar molecules: two molecules of galactose, one molecule of glucose, and one molecule of fructose.

Do You Know? Raffinose is commonly found in various plants, especially in seeds and legumes. It serves as a reserve carbohydrate, providing a source of energy for the growing plant embryo.

Figure 1.1.4 Molecular Structure: (a) sucrose, (b) maltose and (c) lactose 3. Polysaccharides Polysaccharides are complex molecules composed of ten to thousands monosaccharides. They are also known as glycan. Despite their long size, polysaccharides do not function as reducing sugars. They are not water soluble and lack a sweet taste. For example, starch, cellulose, glycogen, and dextrin. Starch serves as a food storage in plants, but animals store it in the form of glycogen, and cellulose is a structural component of plant cell wall. Thus, they can be classified into two functional types:
a. Structural polysaccharides (cellulose in plant cell wall; chitin in fungal cell wall; mannon in yeast cell wall; peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall)
b. Nutrient polysaccharides (starch in plant and bacterial cell, glycogen in animal cell) Based on their composition, they can also be classified into:
a) Homopolysaccharides/homoglycans: They are polymers of only one type of monosaccharide. For example, glucan (made of glucose), fructan (made of fructose).
b) Heteropolysaccharides/heteroglycans: They are polymers of many types of monosaccharide. For example, arabanogalactans.

Figure 1.1.8 Molecular structure of some polysaccharides Activity 1.1 Demonstrate structures of polysaccharide using cotton balls and toothpicks. Differentiate glucose, galactose, and fructose with colored cotton balls. Construct sucrose, maltose, and lactose models, identifying glycosidic bonds. (Optional: Further explore branching in starch and cellulose for a hands-on understanding of polysaccharides.)

Figure 1.1.9 Water colour, cotton and toothpick Materials required: Gather small cotton balls (approximately 1 cm in diameter), three different nontoxic watercolors to represent glucose, galactose, and fructose, and toothpicks Procedure Steps 1 | Color Coding Monosaccharides:
• Soak one cotton ball in each color to represent the three different monosaccharides (glucose, galactose, and fructose).
• Allow the colored cotton balls to dry. Step 2 | Building Disaccharides:
• Use toothpicks to represent glycosidic bonds between the colored cotton balls. • Combine the cotton balls with toothpicks to visually demonstrate the formation of
disaccharides. • For example, use toothpicks to connect glucose and fructose cotton balls to create a model of sucrose.

Functions of Carbohydrates Carbohydrates are essential for various functions in our body:
1. Approximately 50% of our total energy comes from breaking down carbohydrates. 2. Monosaccharides like ribose and deoxyribose are structural elements in nucleic acids.
